common_name: Red Beauty Longspur Epimedium (Deep Red Bicolor Barrenwort)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring or fall in humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in shade to partial shade; Red Beauty is a Darrell Probst selection prized for the deepest, most saturated flower color among the longspur epimediums.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in shade to partial shade. Red Beauty carries wine-red inner sepals set off by slender, white-tipped spurs, a richer, more saturated bicolor combination than the species typically produces, held in loose sprays above foliage that emerges bronze-red before maturing to green. It forms a slowly spreading clump rather than a running mat, so it stays well behaved at the front of a shaded border or along a woodland path. Cut back tattered overwintered foliage in late winter, before the flower spikes push through, so the deep-colored blooms are not hidden.

common_name: Caramel Wushan Epimedium (Caramel-Bronze New Growth Barrenwort)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in shade to partial shade; Caramel is a selected form of the species grown specifically for its richly colored new foliage.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in shade to partial shade, with a little morning sun to intensify new foliage color. Caramel unfurls large, narrowly ovate, spiny-margined evergreen leaflets in a warm caramel-bronze that holds for weeks before settling to dark green, giving this already large-leaved species an extra season of foliage interest. In mid-spring, tall wiry stems carry racemes of pale yellow, long-spurred flowers well above the leathery foliage. It forms a substantial, slow-spreading clump over time and, once established, tolerates the dry shade found under mature trees; comb out old winter foliage before new growth emerges so the spring flowers and fresh caramel leaves are not obscured.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring with the crown at soil level, in humus-rich, evenly moist but well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this hybrid, raised by English plantsman Eric Smith, is grown chiefly for its compact size and rich winter foliage color.

directions: Grow in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, removing tattered old leaves by hand each spring to keep the rosettes tidy. Eric Smith forms a smaller, more compact clump than the coarse species bergenias, with rounded, leathery leaves that flush a deep purple-bronze through cold weather, then sends up dense clusters of carmine-rose flowers on sturdy red stems in early to mid-spring. Its restrained scale suits it to the front of a shaded border, path edging, or a mixed container better than the larger-leaved Bergenia cultivars already common in gardens. Divide congested clumps every four to five years in spring by cutting through the woody, surface-creeping rhizomes.

common_name: Wootton Pink Lamium (Silver-Leaf Bright Pink Dead Nettle)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Wootton Pink is grown for its vivid flower color against silvery foliage, a brighter pink than most other silver-leaved lamium selections.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, away from hot afternoon sun that can scorch the pale foliage. Wootton Pink carries heart-shaped leaves washed almost entirely silver with a narrow green edge, and in late spring produces unusually bright rose-pink flowers that stand out more vividly than the softer lavender-pink tones of most other silver lamium selections. It roots along its trailing stems as it spreads, knitting into a dense, weed-suppressing mat beneath trees and shrubs within a couple of seasons. Shear the planting back lightly after the main flush of bloom to tidy the mat and encourage fresh foliage through summer.

common_name: Jungle Beauty Ajuga (Large Glossy Dark Bronze-Purple Bugleweed)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in partial to full shade; Jungle Beauty is one of the largest-leaved ajuga selections, similar in scale to Catlin's Giant already in this dataset but with darker, glossier foliage.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in partial to full shade. Jungle Beauty produces unusually large, glossy, rounded leaves in a deep bronze-purple that reads almost black in low light, giving mass plantings a bolder visual weight than finer-textured ajuga cultivars. In spring, upright spikes of violet-blue flowers rise well above the foliage and draw early bees to the shade garden. It spreads by surface stolons into a dense, weed-suppressing mat, tolerating root competition and dry shade beneath established trees once settled in; divide and thin congested patches every few years to guard against crown rot in humid conditions.
